### Prerequisites

Before you continue, read the two texts this lesson builds on: **When size matters** (<htcite0>), where we learned to measure an object in one direction with a ruler, and **Comparing in more than one direction** (<htcite1>), where we repeated that measurement in a second direction. This lesson adds the third direction.

text.text:
### Introduction

We have already learned how to measure in two different directions. In **When size matters** we measured the length of an object along a line (<htcite0>), and in **Comparing in more than one direction** we measured length and height and compared both results (<htcite1>). But measuring in two directions is still only part of the comparison: an object can match another in length and height and still be different in the direction we have not measured yet.

Before we continue, look around you. Choose an object near you — a box, a book, a brick or a piece of furniture — and look at it carefully.

source.page: Comparing in more than one direction

text.text:
Reflection 1: How many directions?

We already learned to measure in two different directions. Is that enough to describe the size of the object you just observed? Do you know anything that has fewer than three dimensions?

Everything around us, whether solid, liquid or gas, extends in three directions: length, width and height. These three directions are called the **three dimensions**. The third direction is the one we have not measured yet, and it is the subject of this text.

Before you continue, think about it: a shadow on a wall, a drawing on a sheet of paper or a point on a map can help you think about zero, one or two dimensions, but they are only representations on a surface. In nature, everything that has mass has three dimensions, and the only thing we can see that is not represented in three dimensions is the light, because it has no mass.

### Remembering one direction

A ruler measures **one direction** at a time. Place one end of the object at the **0** mark, keep the object straight along the ruler, and read the number where the other end stops. That number is the measure in that direction. If the object is not straight along the ruler, the number you read will not be the object's true measure. Two objects that stop at the same mark are **equal in that direction**.

A string is long in only one direction, so a single ruler is enough to measure it. Let us measure the blue string and read its length.

#### Practice

Below there is one blue string. Use the **+** and **−** buttons to make it longer or shorter, and watch the ruler under it. The sentence below the string tells you its length in the direction of the ruler.

1
The blue string measures {la} in the direction of the ruler.

### Remembering two directions

Measuring a second direction does not require a new method. Choose the direction, place the object along the ruler starting at **0**, keep it straight, and read the mark where it ends. To measure **length**, we use a horizontal ruler; to measure **height**, a vertical ruler. Then we compare the two measures.

A **square** is the shape whose length and height are equal. Let us practice with one square.

#### Practice

Below there is one blue shape. Use the **+** and **−** buttons to change its length and its height. The rulers show the two measures. Make the shape a square: the length and the height must be equal. Read the sentence that appears below.

1LengthHeight
The blue square has length {l1} and height {h1}. It is a square because the two measures are equal.The blue shape has length {l1} and height {h1}. It is not a square yet because the two measures are different.

### Measuring in three directions

Length, width and height are the three dimensions of a solid object. A **cube** is a solid object whose length, width and height are all equal. Think of an ice cube or a sugar cube: both are cubes.

To measure a cube, use the ruler once for each edge: place the edge along the ruler starting at **0**, keep it straight, and read the mark where it ends. Repeat for the three directions:

1. **Length**: measure the front edge, from left to right.
2. **Width**: measure the side edge, from front to back.
3. **Height**: measure the vertical edge, from bottom to top.

The three measures are the three dimensions of the cube. Two cubes are **fully equal** only when all three measures match. If only one or two measures match, the cubes are equal in those directions but different in the others.

**Figure 1** shows a cube and three rulers, one for each direction. Each ruler starts at 0 and stops at the measure of its edge.
LengthWidthHeight
Figure 1: A cube measured in the three directions: length, width and height.

#### Practice

Below there are two cubes of different sizes. Use the **+** and **−** buttons to change the length, the width and the height of each cube. The rulers around each cube show the three measures; each ruler goes from 0 to 5.

Make the two cubes **fully equal**: all three measures must match. Read the sentence that appears below.

Cube 1LengthWidthHeight
Cube 2LengthWidthHeight
Cube 1 and cube 2 are fully equal: they have the same length ({l1}), the same width ({w1}) and the same height ({h1}).Cube 1 and cube 2 are not fully equal yet: the lengths are {l1} and {l2}, the widths are {w1} and {w2}, and the heights are {h1} and {h2}. Make all three measures match.

### Conclusion

In this text we compared solid objects in three directions. Length, width and height are the three dimensions of a solid object, and a **cube** is an object whose three measures are equal. The practices showed that one or two measures are not enough: two objects are **fully equal** only when they match in every direction we are comparing.

Measuring a cube uses the ruler one direction at a time, and the three measures together describe its size.

As the introduction suggested, everything that has mass around us has three dimensions: shadows, drawings and points are only representations on a surface, and light is the only thing that is not represented in three dimensions. The object you observed at the beginning has three dimensions, and now you can measure each one with a ruler. Comparing all three is what makes our comparison of a solid object complete.
